126 127

ML Algorithms Used in Trading

128

129 Why this matters for HFT_practice: three different learners are 130 already in this repo. fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd uses linear 131 regression. fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd uses a rule (technically not 132 ML — and that matters). paper_trading_sim.py uses 133 GradientBoostingRegressor — the project's flagship model. 134 You should know what each one actually does and why each one lives where it does. 135

136 137 138

1. What does "ML for trading" actually mean in this repo?

139 140

141 Every supervised ML model is a function ŷ = f(x; θ) learned from 142 (input, output) pairs. The art is choosing x, y, 143 and the shape of f. This repo's choice: 144

145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167
VariableIn this projectWhere it's set
x (features)per-day, per-ticker: close, ret_1d, ma_5, ma_10, ma_gap, vol_10, rsi_14build_features in paper_trading_sim.py
y (target)Next day's return, fwd_ret_1d = close.pct_change().shift(-1)same file, line 68
f (model)GradientBoostingRegressor from scikit-learntrain_model, line 113
θ (parameters)The internal weights/tree structure learned from historySaved to models/*.joblib
168 169
170 The single most consequential design choice in the repo: 171 predicting a continuous next-day return (regression), not a 172 direction (up/down classification), not an absolute price. 173 This is why the file is named GradientBoostingRegressor and 174 not ...Classifier. The continuous predictions are then 175 sorted, and the top-N become the portfolio. 176
177 178

The pipeline, from data to dollars

179
180 1 181
Raw data: daily OHLCV from yfinance for every ticker in the universe.
182
183
▼
184
185 2 186
Features: build_features turns prices into returns, moving averages, an MA gap, 10-day vol, RSI. 7 numbers per (ticker, date).
187
188
▼
189
190 3 191
Target: next day's return is shifted into the same row. Training pairs (x, y) ready.
192
193
▼
194
195 4 196
Model: a single GradientBoostingRegressor is fit on the stacked data from all tickers (one model, not one-per-ticker).
197
198
▼
199
200 5 201
Rank & allocate: for each day, predict next-day returns for every ticker, sort, take top_n, send to meanvar_long_only for risk-aware weights.
202
203 204 205

2. The three algorithms in this repo, side by side

206 207
208
209

Linear Regression — small, fast, FPGA-friendly

210

ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ

211

Just a weighted sum. Parametric (fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size). Trained by closed-form least squares.

212

Lives in fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd and the C++ at gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp (despite the filename).

213
214
215

Moving Average Crossover — a rule, not ML

216

Buy when price < (MA − spread). Sell when price > (MA + spread).

217

Zero learned parameters. This is not machine learning — it's a hand-coded mean-reversion rule. Useful baseline to beat.

218

Lives in fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd.

219
220
221

Gradient Boosting Regressor — flagship

222

An ensemble of ~100 small decision trees, where each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones. Non-parametric: model size grows with the data and complexity of the signal.

223

Lives in paper_trading_sim.py:train_model.

224
225
226

Why three? They serve different masters

227

Linear: tiny LUT footprint → FPGA viable. Moving average: zero training data needed → instant baseline. Gradient boosting: best predictive power → wins on the Sharpe ratio, but too big for one chip cycle.

228
229
230 231

What each one can express

232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251 252
ModelCan captureCannot captureTraining data needed
Moving avg ruleMean reversion at one timescaleAnything elseNone
Linear regressionMonotonic, additive effects per featureInteractions, non-linearitiesHundreds of rows
Gradient boostingNon-linear effects, feature interactions, thresholdsVery long-range temporal dependencies (use RNN/transformer for that)Thousands to millions of rows
253 254 255

3. What GradientBoostingRegressor actually does

256 257

258 The name confuses people. Break it down: 259

260
    261
  • "Regressor" = predicts a continuous number (next-day return), not a class.
    • 262
  • "Gradient" = each new tree is trained to predict the gradient of the loss — i.e., the direction the current prediction needs to move. For squared-error loss, that's just the residual.
    • 263
  • "Boosting" = combine many weak learners (shallow trees) sequentially, each one fixing what the previous ensemble got wrong.
    • 264
265 266

Step by step, for the squared-error loss the regressor uses by default:

267 268
269 1 270
Initialize the ensemble prediction at the mean of y: F₀(x) = mean(y_train).
271
272
273 2 274
Compute residuals for every training row: rᵢ = yᵢ − F(xᵢ). These are how far off the current ensemble is on each row.
275
276
277 3 278
Fit a small tree to predict the residuals (depth typically 3–8). The tree carves the feature space into rectangles and predicts a constant residual in each rectangle.
279
280
281 4 282
Add the tree to the ensemble, scaled by a small learning rate (ν, e.g. 0.1): 283 F_new(x) = F(x) + ν · tree(x).
284
285
286 5 287
Repeat from step 2 until you have n_estimators trees (default 100).
288
289 290

291 Final prediction: F(x) = mean(y) + ν · (tree₁(x) + tree₂(x) + … + tree₁₀₀(x)). 292

293 294

295 Why this works for trading returns: each individual tree is too weak to overfit, but 296 the ensemble can compose hundreds of small, non-linear "this feature crosses that 297 threshold AND that other feature is high" rules — exactly the kind of regime-specific 298 signal that a single linear weight can't express. 299

300 301

Tiny, runnable example

302 
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
303	import numpy as np
304	
305	# Toy: 200 days, 2 features (e.g., today's return and 10-day vol)
306	rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
307	X = rng.normal(size=(200, 2))
308	# True signal: positive when feature 0 > 0 AND feature 1 < 0 (an interaction)
309	y = (X[:, 0] > 0) * (X[:, 1] < 0) * 0.02 + rng.normal(0, 0.005, 200)
310	
311	model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1)
312	model.fit(X, y)
313	
314	# Predict and inspect feature importances
315	print(model.predict(X[:5]))
316	print(model.feature_importances_)   # which feature contributes most to splits
317
318 319

320 Linear regression would miss the interaction signal in that toy entirely 321 — it would only see "feature 0 has slight positive correlation" and shrug. 322 Gradient boosting picks up the joint rule because depth-3 trees can split on both 323 features at once. 324

325 326 327

4. In this project

328 329 paper_trading_sim.py (lines 48–69) 330 
def build_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
331	    out = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
332	    out["close"]   = df["Close"]
333	    out["ret_1d"]  = out["close"].pct_change()
334	    out["ma_5"]    = out["close"].rolling(5).mean()
335	    out["ma_10"]   = out["close"].rolling(10).mean()
336	    out["ma_gap"]  = (out["ma_5"] / out["ma_10"]) - 1     # short-vs-long-MA
337	    out["vol_10"]  = out["ret_1d"].rolling(10).std()
338	    out["rsi_14"]  = _rsi(out["close"], 14) / 100.0      # normalized RSI
339	    out["fwd_ret_1d"] = out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)    # THE TARGET — note shift(-1)
340	    return out.dropna()
341
342 343

344 The .shift(-1) on the last line is doing the heavy semantic lifting: 345 it puts tomorrow's return on today's row, so when you train, 346 you're learning "given today's features → predict tomorrow's return." Get that 347 direction wrong and you've built a look-ahead-biased model that looks great in 348 backtests and loses money live. 349

350 351 paper_trading_sim.py (lines 113–125) 352 
def train_model(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> GradientBoostingRegressor:
353	    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42)
354	    model.fit(X, y)
355	    return model
356
357 358

359 Notice what's not here: no hyperparameter tuning, no cross-validation, no 360 regularization knobs explicitly set. sklearn's defaults are 361 n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1, 362 loss="squared_error" — reasonable, conservative starting points for a 363 learner this size. A real production pipeline would sweep these. 364

365 366 paper_trading_sim.py (lines 218–231) — what the prediction is used for 367 
for dt, day_df in pred_df.groupby(level=0):
368	    day_sorted = day_df.sort_values("pred", ascending=False)
369	    picks = day_sorted.head(cfg.top_n)        # <-- rank, take top-N
370	    weight = 1.0 / len(picks)
371	    day_ret = float((picks["fwd_ret_1d"].mean()))   # equal-weight realized return
372
373 374

375 Crucial insight: the model's predicted magnitude barely matters. What 376 matters is its cross-sectional ranking — which tickers it ranks 377 highest today. A model that systematically underestimates returns but still ranks 378 them in the right order will beat a model with low MAE but a noisy ranking. 379

380 381

And on the FPGA: linear regression instead

382 fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd (lines 75–78) 383 
constant W0   : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(  50, 32);   --  0.05 ×1000 — intercept
384	constant W_F0 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 300, 32);   --  0.30 ×1000 — feature 0 weight
385	constant W_F1 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(-100, 32);   -- -0.10 ×1000 — feature 1 weight
386	constant W_F2 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 200, 32);   --  0.20 ×1000 — feature 2 weight
387
388

389 Four numbers. That's the entire model. This is what makes linear 390 regression FPGA-viable: 4 constants → 3 multiplies + 3 adds → done in 2 clock 391 cycles. The 100-tree gradient booster cannot collapse into that. 392

393 394
395 Repo honesty: the Python gradient boosting model is more accurate but 396 can't run on the FPGA. The FPGA linear regression is fast but expresses only a tiny 397 fraction of what the Python model learned. The honest bridge is what fpga/README.md 398 points at: hls4ml or Vitis AI, which compile larger models 399 into HDL by quantizing and pruning. None of that is wired up yet — it's the obvious next 400 step for whoever takes this repo seriously. 401
402 403 404

5. Often confused with

405 406
407
408

Regression vs Classification

409

410 Regression predicts a number on a continuous scale (this repo: 411 next-day return as a decimal). Classification predicts a label 412 (e.g., "up" or "down"). Trading-specific tradeoff: classification throws away 413 magnitude information that is essential for ranking and sizing positions. 414

415
416
417

Gradient Boosting vs Random Forest

418

419 Both are tree ensembles. Random forest trains many independent 420 deep trees on bootstrap samples and averages them — reduces variance. 421 Gradient boosting trains sequential shallow trees, each 422 correcting the previous — reduces bias. Boosting usually wins on tabular data; forests 423 are more robust to bad hyperparameters. 424

425
426
427

Linear Regression vs Logistic Regression

428

429 Linear regression outputs an unbounded number; logistic 430 regression outputs a probability in (0, 1) via a sigmoid. Despite the 431 name, logistic regression is a classifier. This repo uses linear, not 432 logistic. 433

434
435
436

Parametric vs Non-parametric

437

438 Parametric models have a fixed parameter count regardless of data 439 size (linear regression: N weights). Non-parametric models grow 440 with the data (gradient boosting: number and depth of trees scale). 441 Why it matters here: parametric fits an FPGA; non-parametric usually doesn't. 442

443
444
445

Training vs Inference

446

447 Training is the expensive offline step that produces the parameters 448 (model.fit(X, y)). Inference is the cheap online step 449 that uses them (model.predict(X)). HFT cares about inference latency; 450 the model lives or dies on it. Training latency essentially doesn't matter. 451

452
453
454

Feature vs Target

455

456 A feature is what the model sees as input on day T (RSI, MA gap, 457 etc.). The target is what it's trying to predict — here, the return 458 on day T+1. If you accidentally include something from T+1 in the features, you've 459 invented a model that "predicts" what it already knows. That's 460 look-ahead bias and it's the #1 way backtests lie to you. 461

462
463
464 465 466

6. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

467

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

468 469
470

Q1. Why does paper_trading_sim.py use GradientBoostingRegressor and not GradientBoostingClassifier?

471
    472
  • Because sklearn doesn't have a classifier version.
    • 473
  • Because the downstream step ranks tickers by predicted return magnitude to pick top-N — a classifier's up/down labels would discard the magnitude needed for ranking.
    • 474
  • Because classifiers are too slow at inference time.
    • 475
  • Because returns are too noisy for a regressor; a classifier is more accurate.
    • 476
477

478
479 480
481

Q2. In build_features, the line out["fwd_ret_1d"] = out["ret_1d"].shift(-1) — what does the -1 shift accomplish?

482
    483
  • Puts yesterday's return into today's row as a lagged feature.
    • 484
  • Puts tomorrow's return onto today's row, so that one training row pairs today's features with tomorrow's realized return.
    • 485
  • Drops the most recent row from the dataset.
    • 486
  • Normalizes returns by subtracting their lag.
    • 487
488

489
490 491
492

Q3. What does a single tree in GradientBoostingRegressor get trained on, on iteration t?

493
    494
  • The original target y, on a bootstrap sample of rows.
    • 495
  • The residuals (errors) of the current ensemble's predictions — equivalently, the gradient of the loss w.r.t. predictions.
    • 496
  • A random subset of features only, with the original target.
    • 497
  • The output of tree t-1, to mimic the previous tree.
    • 498
499

500
501 502
503

Q4. fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd can run on a single FPGA in ~8 ns. Why isn't the gradient boosting model from paper_trading_sim.py deployed the same way?

504
    505
  • Because trees can only be evaluated one per clock cycle.
    • 506
  • Decision-tree ensembles branch on float comparisons that expand into deep multiplexer trees; 100 trees consume LUT and routing resources that don't fit cleanly on one chip. README points at hls4ml or Vitis AI instead.
    • 507
  • Because FPGAs don't have enough BRAM to hold the tree structures.
    • 508
  • Because scikit-learn models can't be exported to any FPGA toolchain.
    • 509
510

511
512 513
514

Q5. Is fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd machine learning?

515
    516
  • Yes — it computes statistics (the moving average) so it counts as a statistical learning algorithm.
    • 517
  • No — its parameters are hand-chosen at synthesis (WINDOW, SPREAD), not learned from data. It's a fixed mean-reversion rule, useful as a baseline.
    • 518
  • No — but only because it isn't a neural network.
    • 519
  • Yes — anything that produces a buy/sell decision counts as ML.
    • 520
521

522
523 524 525

7. Check your understanding (scenarios)

526 527
528 S1. A teammate adds out["high_today"] = df["High"] to build_features. What's the problem? 529

530 Subtle but lethal: df["High"] is the day's high price, only known 531 after the day closes. Targets are also "after the close" (next day's 532 return). If today's row contains today's high (computed at end-of-day) and you 533 use it to "predict" tomorrow's return, you'd be fine — BUT if you ever apply 534 the model intraday for live trading, you don't yet know today's high, and the 535 live features won't match the training distribution. The model will appear to 536 work in backtest and fail live. Always ask: "would I actually know this feature 537 at the moment I want to act?" 538

539
540 541
542 S2. You sweep n_estimators from 100 → 500 in train_model, and the training R² goes from 0.05 to 0.40 while the test R² drops. What happened, and what would you adjust? 543

544 Classic overfitting: more trees means the ensemble can memorize 545 noise in the training data. The fix is regularization — lower 546 learning_rate (0.05 or 0.03), reduce max_depth (already 3 547 by default — try 2), add subsample=0.8 (stochastic gradient boosting), 548 and use early stopping based on a held-out validation slice. In time-series 549 specifically: never use random k-fold; use a chronological train/validation 550 split or, better, walk-forward — which is exactly what walkforward_sim.py 551 does for evaluation. 552

1	# Glossary — HFT_practice
2	
3	Terms the learner has been introduced to. A term is promoted from *introduced* to
4	*understood* only after they've answered a question about it correctly or used it
5	correctly themselves.
6	
7	Status legend: `intro` = covered in a lesson · `solid` = demonstrably grasped.
8	
9	---
10	
11	### Algorithmic trading — `intro`
12	Any trading where decisions are made by code rather than a human. A superset of HFT.
13	
14	### Ask (offer) — `intro`
15	The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
16	
17	### Adverse selection — `intro`
18	The risk that the counterparty who hit your quote knew more than you did about
19	where the price was about to go. The reason market makers cancel orders aggressively.
20	
21	### Bid — `intro`
22	The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
23	
24	### Colocation — `intro`
25	Renting rack space inside the exchange's data center so your trading server is
26	physically next to the matching engine, minimizing wire latency.
27	
28	### FPGA — `intro`
29	Field-Programmable Gate Array. Reconfigurable hardware wired into a fixed
30	pipeline at synthesis time. Used in HFT for deterministic nanosecond-scale latency.
31	Example in this repo: `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.
32	
33	### HFT (High-Frequency Trading) — `intro`
34	Automated trading defined by microsecond-to-nanosecond latency, very high order
35	rates, and short (often sub-second) holding periods.
36	
37	### Limit order — `intro`
38	"Buy/sell at price X or better." Rests passively in the book until matched or
39	cancelled. The order type market makers post.
40	
41	### Limit Order Book (LOB) — `intro`
42	The full list of resting buy and sell orders at every price level on a venue.
43	The core data structure of modern electronic markets.
44	
45	### Market maker — `intro`
46	A strategy that simultaneously posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread
47	when both sides fill. `fpga/market_maker.vhd` is a hardware example.
48	
49	### Market order — `intro`
50	"Fill me now at the best available price." Crosses the spread and pays for
51	immediacy. The order type takers send.
52	
53	### Mid-price — `intro`
54	`(bid + ask) / 2`. A common reference for "fair value" between the two sides of
55	the book. Computed explicitly in `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.
56	
57	### Q16.16 fixed-point — `intro`
58	A 32-bit signed integer encoding where the lower 16 bits represent the
59	fractional part: `real_value = integer_signal / 65536`. Used in
60	`fpga/market_maker.vhd` so all arithmetic stays in one-cycle integer ops.
61	
62	### Spread — `intro`
63	`ask − bid`. The cost of crossing the book; the prize a market maker tries to
64	capture on round-trips.
65	
66	### Tick — `intro`
67	A single market data update — a trade, a quote change, a cancel. The unit of
68	input to an HFT pipeline.
69	
70	### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
71	The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
72	your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Added in Lesson 0002 (FPGAs in HFT)
77	
78	### ASIC — `intro`
79	Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. Silicon manufactured for one design.
80	Fastest possible, but multi-million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen forever —
81	which is why HFT firms use FPGAs (reconfigurable) instead.
82	
83	### Bitstream — `intro`
84	The binary file produced by synthesis + place-and-route. Loading it onto the
85	FPGA configures every LUT, flip-flop, and routing switch to realize your
86	design. Reloading is a seconds-long operation, not a recompile of a chip.
87	
88	### Combinational logic — `intro`
89	Logic whose outputs depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Inside
90	each pipeline stage in `fpga/*.vhd`, arithmetic between clock edges is
91	combinational.
92	
93	### Determinism (FPGA sense) — `intro`
94	The property that the same input takes the same number of cycles every time.
95	The opposite of CPU jitter from OS scheduling, cache misses, branch prediction.
96	The single biggest reason HFT firms tolerate the pain of FPGA development.
97	
98	### DSP slice — `intro`
99	A dedicated multiply-accumulate block inside the FPGA fabric. Each `*` in
100	VHDL (e.g. `W_F0 * feature_0` in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`) typically
101	maps to one DSP slice.
102	
103	### HDL — `intro`
104	Hardware Description Language. VHDL or Verilog. Describes hardware
105	register-by-register, not as an executing program.
106	
107	### HLS — `intro`
108	High-Level Synthesis. Toolchain that takes annotated C/C++ and generates HDL
109	for you. Faster to write than hand-VHDL; sometimes worse timing or area.
110	`fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl` drives the HLS flow in this repo.
111	
112	### Jitter — `intro`
113	Variability in latency from one event to the next. HFT cares about jitter as
114	much as average latency, because strategies are sized against the worst-case
115	not the median.
116	
117	### Kernel bypass — `intro`
118	Networking techniques (DPDK, Solarflare OpenOnload, XDP) that route packets
119	from the NIC directly to userspace, skipping the Linux kernel network stack.
120	A 20–30% latency win for CPU-based HFT; obsolete on FPGA NICs where parsing
121	is on-chip already.
122	
123	### LUT (Look-Up Table) — `intro`
124	The basic configurable unit of FPGA fabric. A small truth table that can be
125	programmed to compute any function of N inputs (typically N=6). LUT count is
126	the headline capacity metric of an FPGA part.
127	
128	### Pipeline stage — `intro`
129	A combinational chunk of logic terminated by a register (flip-flop). More
130	stages = higher clock frequency but more cycles of latency. `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
131	has 2 stages; `market_maker.vhd` has 1.
132	
133	### Place-and-Route (PAR) — `intro`
134	The step after synthesis that assigns each gate in your netlist to a physical
135	LUT on the chip and routes the wires between them. Where timing closure is
136	won or lost.
137	
138	### Sequential logic — `intro`
139	Logic that uses flip-flops driven by a clock to hold state between cycles.
140	Each pipeline stage boundary in the repo's VHDL is sequential.
141	
142	### Synthesis — `intro`
143	The step that turns HDL source into a netlist of generic gates. Distinct from
144	Place-and-Route, which maps those gates onto the physical chip.
145	
146	### Timing closure — `intro`
147	The act of making your design meet the target clock period at every register-
148	to-register path. The real bottleneck of FPGA HFT development — not the
149	arithmetic, not the algorithm, but proving the silicon can run that fast.
150	
151	### Valid handshake — `intro`
152	The convention of carrying a `valid` bit alongside every datum through a
153	pipeline, so each stage knows which cycles contain real data. Used uniformly
154	in all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules.
155	
156	### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
157	Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
158	in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
159	firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## Added in Lesson 0003 (ML Algorithms in Trading)
164	
165	### Boosting — `intro`
166	Sequentially combine many weak learners (typically shallow trees), each trained
167	to correct the errors of the previous ensemble. Contrast with bagging
168	(independent learners averaged together).
169	
170	### Classification vs Regression — `intro`
171	**Classification** predicts a discrete label (up/down). **Regression** predicts
172	a continuous number. This repo uses regression because the downstream step
173	ranks tickers by predicted-return magnitude, which requires the number itself.
174	
175	### Cross-sectional ranking — `intro`
176	At each date, rank all tickers by their predicted return and act on the top-N.
177	The model's predicted *magnitude* matters less than its *order*. The whole
178	selection step in `paper_trading_sim.py` (`sort_values("pred")`) depends on this.
179	
180	### Ensemble — `intro`
181	A model made of many sub-models combined to produce one prediction.
182	`GradientBoostingRegressor`'s default is 100 trees combined additively with a
183	0.1 learning rate.
184	
185	### Feature engineering — `intro`
186	Turning raw data into model inputs. In this repo: returns, moving averages,
187	MA gap, rolling vol, RSI — all computed in `build_features` from raw Close prices.
188	
189	### Gradient Boosting — `intro`
190	A boosting method where each new weak learner is fit to the gradient of the
191	loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions. For squared error,
192	the gradient is just the residual `y − F(x)`, so each tree learns the current
193	error pattern.
194	
195	### GradientBoostingRegressor — `intro`
196	scikit-learn's class for gradient-boosted decision trees on a continuous target.
197	The flagship model in `paper_trading_sim.py:train_model`.
198	
199	### Inference — `intro`
200	Applying a trained model to make predictions (`model.predict(X)`). The
201	latency-sensitive half of ML — what HFT cares about almost exclusively.
202	
203	### Learning rate (ν) — `intro`
204	The scalar that scales each new tree's contribution before adding it to the
205	ensemble. Smaller = more conservative updates, more trees needed, better
206	generalization. Default 0.1 in sklearn.
207	
208	### Linear Regression — `intro`
209	`ŷ = w₀ + Σ wᵢ xᵢ`. Closed-form least-squares fit. Parametric, additive, fast.
210	Used in `fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd` because four constants fit in
211	silicon trivially.
212	
213	### Look-ahead bias — `intro`
214	The bug where a feature secretly contains information from the future relative
215	to the target. Backtests look great; live trading loses money. The
216	`.shift(-1)` discipline in `build_features` is what prevents this when done
217	correctly.
218	
219	### Mean-variance optimization — `intro`
220	Markowitz's portfolio framework: choose weights `w` to balance expected return
221	`μᵀw` against risk `wᵀΣw`. Closed-form long-only solution `w ∝ Σ⁻¹μ` is
222	implemented in `predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only`. Not ML — it's optimization
223	on top of the ML output.
224	
225	### Non-parametric model — `intro`
226	A model whose effective parameter count grows with the data. Gradient-boosted
227	trees are non-parametric in this sense. Contrast: linear regression's
228	parameter count is fixed at N+1 regardless of dataset size.
229	
230	### Overfitting — `intro`
231	When a model fits noise in the training data and fails to generalize to new
232	data. In `GradientBoostingRegressor` it appears as training R² climbing while
233	test R² drops. Fixes: lower learning rate, shallower trees, more
234	regularization, early stopping.
235	
236	### Parametric model — `intro`
237	A model with a fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size. Linear
238	regression: N feature weights plus an intercept, done. Parametric models are
239	much easier to fit on an FPGA.
240	
241	### Residual — `intro`
242	`y − F(x)` — what the current ensemble got wrong on a given row. Gradient
243	boosting fits each new tree to predict the residuals of the previous step.
244	
245	### RSI (Relative Strength Index) — `intro`
246	A 0–100 momentum oscillator that rises when up-days dominate down-days within
247	the lookback window. Computed in `paper_trading_sim._rsi` with window=14 and
248	normalized to 0–1 in `build_features`.
249	
250	### Supervised learning — `intro`
251	Learning a mapping from inputs `x` to known outputs `y`, using a dataset of
252	labeled examples. All three "ML" elements in this repo (linear regression and
253	gradient boosting) are supervised. The MA rule in VHDL is *not* supervised —
254	it isn't learned at all.
255	
256	### Target — `intro`
257	The value the model is trained to predict. In this repo: `fwd_ret_1d`, the
258	next-day return, computed via `out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)`.
259	
260	### Training vs Inference — `intro`
261	**Training** is the expensive offline step that produces parameters (`fit`).
262	**Inference** is the cheap online step that uses them (`predict`). HFT cares
263	about inference latency; training latency essentially doesn't matter.

265	---
266	
267	## Added in Lesson 0004 (Linux Internal Networking)
268	
269	### 0.0.0.0 (wildcard bind) — `intro`
270	A wildcard address meaning "listen on every interface in this network
271	namespace." Used in this repo's `Dockerfile`. Distinct from `127.0.0.1`,

273	
274	### Bridge (Linux bridge) — `intro`

293	### eth0 (container) — `intro`
294	The conventional name of a container's primary virtual ethernet interface.
295	One end of a veth pair; the other end sits on the host bridge.
296	
297	### iptables / Netfilter — `intro`
298	The Linux kernel's packet-filtering and NAT framework. Docker programs it to
299	implement port forwarding (DNAT) and outbound source rewriting (MASQUERADE).
300	
301	### Kernel bypass — `solid` (promoted from intro in Lesson 0002)
302	Skipping the kernel network stack to cut tick-to-trade latency. DPDK,
303	OpenOnload, XDP are CPU-side; FPGA NICs go further by doing parsing in
304	hardware.
305	
306	### Loopback (`lo`, 127.0.0.1) — `intro`
307	A virtual interface inside the kernel where packets never reach any NIC.
308	Every network namespace has its own private loopback — the container's
309	`127.0.0.1` is not the host's `127.0.0.1`.
310	
311	### MASQUERADE / SNAT — `intro`
312	iptables rule that rewrites the source IP of outbound packets. Used by Docker
313	so that traffic from a container's private bridge IP appears to come from the
314	host's outbound IP, so replies can route back correctly.
315	
316	### Namespace (network namespace) — `intro`
317	A kernel object that gives a group of processes their own copy of the network
318	stack: their own interfaces, routing table, iptables rules, loopback. The
319	isolation primitive containers are built on.
320	
321	### Network stack (Linux) — `intro`
322	The kernel's layered TCP/IP implementation: socket layer → TCP/UDP → IP →
323	netfilter → qdisc → driver. Each layer adds latency; total is typically
324	~50–120 µs round-trip on a busy host.
325	
326	### Port — `intro`
327	A 16-bit number that distinguishes endpoints on a host. Part of the socket
328	5-tuple `(proto, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port)`.
329	
330	### Port forwarding — `intro`
331	Common name for DNAT-based "expose container port X on host port Y." What
332	`ports: "8000:8000"` in `docker-compose.yml` actually does.
333	
334	### Qdisc (Queueing discipline) — `intro`
335	The kernel's packet-scheduling layer between the IP layer and the NIC driver.
336	Decides which packet goes out next when the wire is busy.
337	
338	### Socket — `intro`
339	The kernel object representing one endpoint of a connection, identified by
340	the 5-tuple. A listening socket can spawn many connected sockets, all sharing
341	one port.
342	
343	### TCP/UDP — `intro`
344	The two main L4 transports. TCP is reliable, ordered, connection-oriented.
345	UDP is unreliable, unordered, connectionless. Exchange market data is almost
346	always UDP (multicast); orders are usually TCP-based protocols like FIX.
347	
348	### veth pair — `intro`
349	A pair of virtual ethernet interfaces in the kernel, connected back-to-back.
350	Packets out one end appear at the other. Docker uses veth pairs to bridge a
351	container's network namespace to the host bridge.

355	## Added in Lesson 0005 (Prediction Models in Trading)
356	
357	### Adaptivity (model) — `intro`
358	Whether a model is trained once (`paper_trading_sim.py`) or refit periodically
359	on rolling windows (`walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain`). One of the five
360	axes that define a trading prediction model.
361	
362	### Cross-sectional model — `intro`
363	A model that ranks N assets against each other at the same point in time.
364	This repo's GBM is cross-sectional: every day it scores all tickers and picks
365	the top-N. Contrast with time-series, which forecasts one asset's future from
366	its own past.
367	
368	### Cross-sectional pooling — `intro`
369	Training one model on rows from many assets stacked together, assuming the
370	feature→target relationship is roughly universal. The repo does this; sector
371	or market-cap bucketing is the production refinement.
372	
373	### CUSUM (cumulative sum) — `intro`
374	A change-point detection statistic. Triggers when the cumulative deviation of
375	a series from its mean exceeds a threshold. Used in `walkforward_sim.py` as
376	one of four stress detectors that gate exposure.
377	
378	### Distributional forecast — `intro`
379	A prediction that includes uncertainty — quantiles, mean+variance, or a full
380	distribution. Lets downstream sizing be risk-aware. This repo currently
381	emits only point estimates.
382	
383	### Filtering (vs forecasting) — `intro`
384	Estimating a *present* hidden state from past observations (HMM/GMM regime
385	detection). Distinct from forecasting, which estimates a *future* value. The
386	repo's `GaussianMixture` overlay is filtering, not forecasting.
387	
388	### Foundation model (time-series) — `intro`
389	Large pretrained model (TimesFM, Chronos, Kronos, Moirai) trained on billions
390	of time-series points, used for zero-/few-shot forecasting. On tabular daily
391	equity features, GBM still beats them for cross-sectional ranking — for now.
392	
393	### Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — `intro`
394	A probabilistic clustering model that fits K Gaussian components to a dataset.
395	Used in `walkforward_sim.py` to estimate the probability that today's returns
396	belong to a "high-vol" regime, then to scale exposure down accordingly.
397	
398	### Hidden Markov Model (HMM) — `intro`
399	A state-space model where an unobserved discrete state evolves over time and
400	emits observations. Common as a regime model in finance. The repo's GMM is a
401	simpler cousin (no transition matrix — just clustering).
402	
403	### Horizon (forecast horizon) — `intro`
404	The future window over which the target is measured. This repo: 1 trading
405	day. Choose tick-level and you need a completely different infrastructure.
406	
407	### Output shape — `intro`
408	The form of a model's prediction: point estimate, distribution, or action.
409	One of the five axes; the repo emits point estimates only.
410	
411	### Per-asset model — `intro`
412	One model per ticker, trained on that ticker's data only. Opposite of
413	cross-sectional pooling. Captures asset-specific quirks but starves on
414	data and fails for new tickers.
415	
416	### Pooling (model pooling) — `intro`
417	The choice between training one shared model across assets vs one per asset.
418	One of the five axes; this repo pools across all tickers.
419	
420	### Regime model — `intro`
421	Any model whose primary output is the identification of a hidden market state
422	(calm/stress, bull/bear). Used to switch strategies or scale exposure, not to
423	predict returns directly. `walkforward_sim.py:GaussianMixture` is the
424	project's regime model.
425	
426	### Reinforcement learning (in trading) — `intro`
427	Learning an action policy directly from a reward signal (P&L). Promising for
428	execution and market-making but notoriously hard to train on financial data.
429	Not used in this repo.
430	
431	### Rolling retrain — `intro`
432	Periodically refitting a model on a fixed-length window of the most recent
433	past data only. `walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain --retrain_freq monthly
434	--train_window_days 756` is the repo's default flavor.
435	
436	### Stationarity — `intro`
437	A property of a time series whose statistical moments don't drift over time.
438	Returns are roughly stationary; prices are not. Pooling across tickers
439	requires features and targets that are at least approximately stationary —
440	this is why the repo predicts returns, not prices.
441	
442	### Target axis — `intro`
443	The choice of what the model predicts: direction (binary), magnitude
444	(regression), volatility, jump probability, regime, or action (RL). The
445	single most consequential design decision in a trading model.
446	
447	### TimesFM / Chronos / Kronos — `intro`
448	Time-series foundation models from the 2024–2025 wave (Google, Amazon,
449	Tsinghua respectively). Pretrained transformers for general forecasting.
450	Strong zero-shot on benchmarks; not yet a slam-dunk on tabular cross-sectional
451	equity alpha.

455	## Added in Lesson 0006 (Statistics Math in Trading)
456	
457	### Annualization factor — `intro`
458	Convention for converting per-period statistics to per-year. For US equities,
459	252 trading days. Means scale by ×252; standard deviations scale by ×√252
460	(because variances add across independent periods).
461	
462	### Bessel's correction (ddof=1) — `intro`
463	Dividing by (n−1) instead of n when computing sample variance/std, to get an
464	unbiased estimator. pandas defaults to `ddof=1`; NumPy defaults to `ddof=0`.
465	Cross-library default mismatches are a real bug source.
466	
467	### CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) — `intro`
468	Geometric annual return: `(final / initial)^(252/N) − 1`. The actual
469	compounded growth rate. Always ≤ arithmetic APR; gap is volatility drag.
470	Computed in `analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics`.
471	
472	### Correlation — `intro`
473	Standardized covariance: `cov(i,j) / (σᵢ σⱼ)`. Unit-free, bounded in [−1, 1].
474	Use for comparing relationships across assets; covariance for portfolio
475	variance formulas.
476	
477	### Covariance matrix (Σ) — `intro`
478	Symmetric matrix whose entry (i,j) is the covariance of asset i and asset j
479	returns. Diagonal entries are variances. The repo estimates Σ from the recent
480	`--cov_lookback` days in `predict_next.py:compute_returns`.
481	
482	### CUSUM (cumulative sum) test — `intro`
483	Change-point statistic that tracks deviations from the mean. Two running sums
484	(positive and negative drift) update each period with a slack term k. The
485	repo uses `k = cusum_threshold * σ` (default 3σ) as one of four stress
486	detectors in `walkforward_sim.py`.
487	
488	### Drawdown — `intro`
489	Percentage drop from the running peak so far:
490	`DD_t = equity_t / max_{s≤t}(equity_s) − 1`. Always ≤ 0.
491	
492	### Log return — `intro`
493	`ln(P_t / P_{t-1})`. Sums across time linearly; symmetric around zero. Used in
494	academic risk math. Numerically ≈ simple return for small moves.
495	
496	### Maximum drawdown (MaxDD) — `intro`
497	The minimum of the drawdown series over the full period — the worst
498	peak-to-trough loss the equity curve ever felt. Investors emotionally trade on
499	this number more than on Sharpe.
500	
501	### Sharpe ratio — `intro`
502	Risk-adjusted return: `(mean_return × 252) / (std_return × √252)`. Unit-free.
503	This repo's version assumes risk-free rate = 0. >1 solid, >2 excellent, >3
504	raises eyebrows.
505	
506	### Shrinkage (covariance) — `intro`
507	Mixing the sample covariance matrix with a more stable target (typically the
508	diagonal): `Σ_shrunk = (1−λ) Σ_sample + λ diag(Σ_sample)`. Trades a little
509	bias for much less estimation noise; vital when Σ is going to be inverted.
510	Lives in `predict_next.py` via `--shrink`.
511	
512	### Simple return — `intro`
513	`(P_t − P_{t-1}) / P_{t-1}`. Computed by pandas `.pct_change()`. Aggregates
514	linearly across *assets* in a portfolio: `r_p = Σ wᵢ rᵢ`. This repo's
515	default everywhere.
516	
517	### Sortino ratio — `intro`
518	Like Sharpe but divides by downside standard deviation only (negative returns
519	counted, positive ignored). Kinder to positively skewed strategies. Not
520	computed in this repo.
521	
522	### Standard deviation (σ) — `intro`
523	Square root of variance. Same units as the underlying. In finance: "volatility."
524	
525	### Variance — `intro`
526	`E[(r − μ)²]`. Units: returns². Adds linearly across independent periods,
527	which is why annual std = daily std × √252.
528	
529	### Volatility drag — `intro`
530	The gap between arithmetic and geometric mean return, approximately σ²/2 in
531	log terms. A high-vol strategy with the same mean as a low-vol one will
532	compound *more slowly*. The reason `analyze_equity.py` returns both
533	`APR_simple` and `CAGR`.

537	## Added in Lesson 0007 (Neural Networks in Quant)
538	
539	### Activation function — `intro`
540	The elementwise nonlinearity inside each NN layer (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU).
541	Without it, a stack of linear layers collapses to one linear layer.
542	
543	### Attention / self-attention — `intro`
544	The mechanism at the heart of transformers: each output position is a weighted
545	combination of all input positions, with weights computed from the inputs
546	themselves. Replaces the sequential recurrence of an LSTM.
547	
548	### Backpropagation — `intro`
549	The chain-rule algorithm that computes gradients of a loss with respect to
550	every weight in a network. Combined with an optimizer (Adam, SGD) it's how
551	neural nets train.
552	
553	### BERT / FinBERT — `intro`
554	BERT is a 2018 transformer pretrained on text via masked-language-modeling.
555	FinBERT is BERT fine-tuned on financial corpora (news, filings). Alpha
556	Vantage's news sentiment is a BERT-family model's output.
557	
558	### CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) — `intro`
559	NN that applies learned filters across local windows of its input. Dominant
560	on images and the 2D price-level grid of LOB snapshots (DeepLOB).
561	
562	### Deep RL — `intro`
563	Reinforcement learning where the policy and/or value function is a neural
564	network. Used in quant for execution and market-making research; production
565	deployment is rare due to backtesting difficulty.
566	
567	### DeepLOB / TransLOB / TLOB — `intro`
568	Neural architectures for limit-order-book modeling. DeepLOB (2018): CNN+LSTM
569	on LOB snapshots. TransLOB / TLOB (2024–2025): transformer variants with
570	attention over price levels. The natural NN bridge to this repo's FPGA work.
571	
572	### Embedding — `intro`
573	A learned dense vector representation of a discrete input (a word, a ticker,
574	an article). The intermediate layer outputs of a transformer are embeddings
575	of the input — much richer than a single scalar like a sentiment score.
576	
577	### Epoch / Iteration / Batch — `intro`
578	**Batch**: a chunk of training rows for one gradient step. **Iteration**: one
579	batch processed. **Epoch**: one full pass through the training set.
580	
581	### Feedforward / MLP — `intro`
582	A neural network where every layer is fully connected and information flows
583	forward only (no recurrence, no attention). The simplest deep NN.
584	
585	### Fine-tuning — `intro`
586	Taking a pretrained model and continuing training on a smaller task-specific
587	dataset. FinBERT is BERT fine-tuned on financial text.
588	
589	### Gradient descent (in NN context) — `intro`
590	The optimizer that updates weights `W ← W − η·∇L` to reduce the loss.
591	Variants (Adam, RMSprop, SGD with momentum) differ in how they adapt the
592	step size per weight.
593	
594	### hls4ml — `intro`
595	Open-source toolchain that compiles trained scikit-learn/Keras/PyTorch models
596	into HDL for FPGA deployment. Documented in `fpga/README.md` as the bridge
597	from the Python model side to the silicon side.
598	
599	### Linear collapse — `intro`
600	The fact that the composition of linear functions is linear. Stacking N
601	linear layers without nonlinearities is mathematically equivalent to one
602	linear layer.
603	
604	### LSTM / GRU — `intro`
605	Recurrent NN cells designed to remember information across long sequences
606	via gating. State-of-the-art for sequence forecasting from ~2016–2022;
607	now often replaced by transformers.
608	
609	### Loss function — `intro`
610	The scalar objective the optimizer minimizes. MSE for regression, cross-entropy
611	for classification, Huber for robustness. Distinct from the activation function.
612	
613	### Neural network — `intro`
614	A stack of (linear transform → nonlinearity) layers, trained by minimizing a
615	loss with gradient-based optimization. Not used in this repo's Python code
616	today, but Alpha Vantage's sentiment score is one consumed silently.
617	
618	### Pretraining — `intro`
619	Training a large model on a huge generic corpus before any task-specific
620	training. The base half of "pretrain + fine-tune."
621	
622	### ReLU — `intro`
623	Rectified Linear Unit: `max(0, x)`. The default activation function in
624	modern feedforward networks. Cheap to compute, mostly avoids vanishing
625	gradients.
626	
627	### RNN / Recurrent NN — `intro`
628	NN that processes a sequence step-by-step, carrying hidden state forward.
629	LSTM and GRU are RNN cells designed to mitigate vanishing gradients.
630	
631	### Transformer — `intro`
632	NN architecture built on self-attention; processes all sequence positions in
633	parallel. Dominant in NLP, increasingly in finance time-series (TLOB,
634	TimesFM, Chronos, Kronos).
635	
636	### Universal Approximation Theorem — `intro`
637	A theoretical guarantee that a NN with one sufficiently wide hidden layer can
638	approximate any continuous function. Comfort, not a recipe — depth is what
639	makes networks practically trainable on real data.

643	## Added in Lesson 0008 (LLM Use-Cases in HFT)
644	
645	### Agent (LLM agent) — `intro`
646	LLM that plans → calls a tool → reads result → plans next step, in a loop.
647	Useful for open-ended research; brittle in production. Failure modes include
648	infinite loops and confident wrongness.
649	
650	### Alpha-GPT — `intro`
651	Class of research systems (2024–2025) that use LLMs with prompt engineering
652	to propose trading signal code, then backtest the result. Promising as an
653	exploration loop, not as an autonomous trader.
654	
655	### Cold path / Warm path / Hot path — `intro`
656	Three latency regimes for LLM-relevance in a trading firm.
657	**Hot path** (ns–µs, FPGA/CPU tick-to-trade): LLMs forbidden.
658	**Warm path** (ms–s, intraday research/alerts): LLMs sometimes.
659	**Cold path** (seconds+, overnight research/docs): LLMs obvious.
660	
661	### Completion model — `intro`
662	LLM endpoint that generates text given a prompt. Distinct from an *embedding*
663	model, which produces vectors for similarity search.
664	
665	### Distillation (LLM) — `intro`
666	Training a small model to mimic input/output pairs of a frontier model.
667	Get most of the quality at a fraction of cost. Standard for high-volume
668	feature-extraction jobs (e.g. scoring millions of articles).
669	
670	### Embedding model — `intro`
671	LLM endpoint that turns text into a dense vector for similarity search.
672	The retrieval half of RAG.
673	
674	### Fine-tuning (LLM) — `intro`
675	Continuing training of a base LLM on task-specific data. Changes the model's
676	weights. Slower to update than RAG; usually justified only with abundant
677	labeled examples and a single repeatable task.
678	
679	### Function calling / Tool use — `intro`
680	The protocol whereby an LLM emits a structured request to call a specific
681	function on the host (e.g. `compute_metrics(equity_csv)`), then incorporates
682	the result into its final answer. Lets the LLM stay symbolic and accurate.
683	
684	### Hallucination — `intro`
685	The model fabricates a fact (a paper, a function, a citation) that doesn't
686	exist. Distinct from being wrong about a real fact. Both look the same to the
687	user; both demand verification before acting.
688	
689	### Hosted vs Self-hosted LLM — `intro`
690	**Hosted**: API call to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google. Cheap per call, no infra.
691	**Self-hosted**: run an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek)
692	on your own GPUs. Mandatory for sensitive data; cheaper at scale.
693	
694	### LLM (Large Language Model) — `intro`
695	Transformer-architecture neural network with 10⁹–10¹² parameters, pretrained
696	on internet-scale text. Larger cousins of BERT/FinBERT from Lesson 0007.
697	General-purpose; expensive per call; cannot sit on the HFT hot path.
698	
699	### MCP (Model Context Protocol) — `intro`
700	2024–2025 open standard for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to LLMs.
701	The agreed-upon plumbing layer between an LLM client and your codebase.
702	
703	### Prompt engineering — `intro`
704	Writing inputs to an LLM that reliably produce useful structured outputs.
705	Includes system prompts, few-shot examples, format constraints (JSON mode),
706	chain-of-thought instructions.
707	
708	### RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — `intro`
709	Pattern where relevant chunks of an external corpus are retrieved at query
710	time and stuffed into the LLM's context. Default architecture for codebase
711	or document Q&A; cheap, deterministic-ish, no fine-tuning required.
712	
713	### StockBench — `intro`
714	2025 benchmark for LLM agents trading real-world stock data. Headline result:
715	most LLM agents underperform buy-and-hold. Implication: LLMs are tools, not
716	traders.
717	
718	### System prompt vs User prompt — `intro`
719	**System**: the persistent instruction set ("you are a quant assistant").
720	**User**: the per-query message. Mixing them weakens guardrails.
721	
722	### Temperature — `intro`
723	The decoding parameter controlling sampling randomness. `temperature=0` gives
724	deterministic-ish output (still subject to provider model changes). Always
725	use 0 for feature pipelines that need to be reproducible.
726	
727	### Vector store — `intro`
728	A database (FAISS, sqlite-vss, Pinecone, pgvector) that indexes embeddings
729	and supports nearest-neighbor retrieval. The R in RAG.

733	## Added in Lesson 0009 (Low-Latency C++ for Trading)
734	
735	### Atomic (operation) — `intro`
736	A single hardware-level read/modify/write instruction (CAS, LOCK XADD) that
737	is indivisible. ~25 ns. Building block of lock-free queues.
738	
739	### Branch elimination — `intro`
740	Rewriting code so a conditional is replaced by arithmetic
741	(`x = cond*a + (1-cond)*b`). Worth it when the branch is unpredictable.
742	
743	### Branch prediction — `intro`
744	The CPU's front-end guesses which side of a conditional will be taken before
745	the comparison resolves. Mispredict cost ~10–20 ns (pipeline flush).
746	
747	### Cache line — `intro`
748	The unit the CPU fetches from main memory: 64 bytes on modern x86. Reading
749	one byte fetches the whole line; sequential access is cheap, random access
750	across lines is expensive.
751	
752	### Cache (L1/L2/L3) — `intro`
753	On-die SRAM hierarchy. L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~3 ns, L3 ~15 ns. The 100× gap to main
754	memory (~100 ns) makes "is the working set cache-resident?" the most
755	important performance question.
756	
757	### Constexpr — `intro`
758	C++ keyword guaranteeing a value or function is evaluable at compile time.
759	Lets the compiler fold the value into the generated machine code as an
760	immediate instead of a runtime memory load.
761	
762	### CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) — `intro`
763	Static-polymorphism idiom: a base class is templated on the derived type so
764	all dispatch is resolved at compile time. Replaces virtual functions in
765	HFT-grade C++.
766	
767	### False sharing — `intro`
768	When two threads write different variables that happen to share a cache
769	line, the line ping-pongs between caches and performance collapses. Fix
770	with `alignas(64)` padding.
771	
772	### Hot path / Cold path — `intro`
773	**Hot path**: the per-tick code that runs millions of times a second. No
774	allocation, no I/O, no syscalls. **Cold path**: setup, teardown, rare
775	events. Allocate, log, and call APIs freely.
776	
777	### Inlining — `intro`
778	Compiler optimization that replaces a function call with the function body.
779	Removes call/ret overhead and enables cross-boundary optimization. Templates
780	inline; non-final `virtual` calls do not.
781	
782	### `[[likely]]` / `[[unlikely]]` — `intro`
783	C++20 attributes that hint to the compiler which branch is the common case.
784	Help with code layout and icache pressure; do not replace the hardware
785	predictor.
786	
787	### Lock-free queue / SPSC ring — `intro`
788	A fixed-size circular buffer where a single producer thread writes and a
789	single consumer thread reads using only atomic head/tail indices — no
790	mutex. The HFT-grade alternative to `std::cout` from the hot path.
791	
792	### `noexcept` — `intro`
793	Function specifier promising no exceptions will escape. Lets the compiler
794	skip generating unwinding scaffolding and inline more aggressively. Default
795	on every leaf hot-path function.
796	
797	### Pipeline (CPU pipeline) — `intro`
798	The CPU executes instructions in ~15 overlapping stages. A branch mispredict
799	or a long-latency memory access stalls the pipeline. Modern HFT C++ is
800	largely about avoiding pipeline stalls.
801	
802	### Ring buffer (stack) — `intro`
803	A fixed-size circular array used as a FIFO. O(1) push/pop, no allocation.
804	The C++ analog of the VHDL `price_reg` shift register in
805	`fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd`.
806	
807	### SoA vs AoS — `intro`
808	**Struct-of-Arrays**: one array per field (`prices[]`, `volumes[]`). Fast
809	when iterating one field at a time. **Array-of-Structs**: one record per
810	row (`struct Tick { p; v; }`). Fast when touching multiple fields together.
811	HFT often prefers SoA for vectorization.
812	
813	### Spinlock — `intro`
814	A lock that busy-waits via CAS instead of sleeping. Uncontended ~25 ns;
815	contended catastrophically slow. Used only when expected hold time is
816	shorter than a kernel sleep cycle.
817	
818	### Stack vs Heap allocation — `intro`
819	**Stack**: pointer move, fixed size, free. **Heap** (`new`, `malloc`,
820	`vector::push_back`): unpredictable, allocator-locked, ~30–200 ns. Hot-path
821	code lives on the stack and on pre-allocated arenas.
822	
823	### Syscall — `intro`
824	A user-to-kernel transition (`read`, `write`, `mmap`). Cheapest is ~300 ns;
825	many are much more. Treated as the boundary of "fast code" — hot loops
826	never cross it.
827	
828	### Vtable / Virtual call — `intro`
829	The dispatch table backing `virtual` methods. Each call requires a pointer
830	load and an indirect jump (~5–15 ns) and, more importantly, blocks the
831	compiler from inlining. Replaced by templates/CRTP in HFT code.

839	Used on SPSC ring head/tail indices to prevent false sharing between
840	producer and consumer cores.
841	
842	### Busy polling (CPU side) — `intro`
843	Spin in user space calling `_mm_pause()` on the data source (a ring, a NIC
844	queue) instead of sleeping. Near-zero wakeup latency; burns one core at
845	100% utilization. Used on the strategy thread; not on the logger.
846	
847	### Cache coherence / Line ping-pong — `intro`
848	When two cores repeatedly write to the same cache line, the line bounces
849	between their L1 caches via the L3 (~30 ns per round-trip). The performance
850	killer that `alignas(64)` defends against.
851	
852	### CPU isolation (`isolcpus`) — `intro`
853	Linux kernel boot parameter that tells the scheduler to leave specific
854	cores free of general tasks. Combined with `nohz_full` (no timer tick) and
855	`rcu_nocbs` (no RCU callbacks) for true HFT-grade isolation.
856	
857	### `_mm_pause()` — `intro`
858	x86 intrinsic that hints to the CPU that this is a spin-wait loop. Slows
859	speculative execution, conserves power, friendlier to a sibling
860	hyperthread. Always used in tight polling loops.
861	
862	### Lock-free vs Wait-free — `intro`
863	**Lock-free**: at least one thread always makes progress. **Wait-free**:
864	every thread completes in bounded steps. A correct SPSC ring with the
865	above pattern is wait-free; most MPMC queues are only lock-free.
866	
867	### LTO (Link-Time Optimization) — `intro`
868	Compiler flag (`-flto`) that runs the optimizer at link time across all
869	translation units, enabling cross-TU inlining and dead-code elimination.
870	Stacks with PGO.
871	
872	### `mlockall` — `intro`
873	Linux syscall that locks all of a process's pages into RAM, preventing the
874	kernel from paging them out. Used in HFT setups so a memory page fault
875	can't introduce ms-scale jitter.
876	
877	### `memory_order_acquire` — `intro`
878	Atomic load ordering that pairs with `release` on the other side. Ensures
879	all reads after the acquire-load see writes done before the matching
880	release-store. Used by the SPSC consumer reading `head_`.
881	
882	### `memory_order_relaxed` — `intro`
883	Atomic operation with no synchronization — only atomicity. Cheapest. Used
884	when the thread owns the variable (e.g. the producer reading its own
885	`head_`).
886	
887	### `memory_order_release` — `intro`
888	Atomic store ordering. Guarantees all writes done before the store are
889	visible to a thread that acquire-loads the same atomic. The "publish" in
890	SPSC.
891	
892	### `memory_order_seq_cst` — `intro`
893	Atomic ordering that gives a total global order over all seq_cst
894	operations. Default in `std::atomic`. ~5–10 ns overhead on x86
895	(MFENCE). Avoid unless you actually need it.
896	
897	### `nohz_full` — `intro`
898	Linux boot parameter that disables the 1 kHz scheduling timer on isolated
899	cores when only one task is runnable. Removes ~1000 interrupts/sec of
900	jitter from the HFT hot path.
901	
902	### MPSC / MPMC queue — `intro`
903	**MPSC**: multi-producer, single-consumer (e.g. many threads feeding one
904	logger). **MPMC**: multi-producer, multi-consumer. Both are more expensive
905	than SPSC; design the system to need SPSC wherever possible.
906	
907	### PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization) — `intro`
908	Build twice: first with `-fprofile-generate` to instrument, run a
909	representative workload, then rebuild with `-fprofile-use` so the compiler
910	knows which branches are hot. 5–15% latency wins on the hot path.
911	
912	### `pthread_setaffinity_np` — `intro`
913	POSIX call that pins a thread to a specific CPU core via a `cpu_set_t`
914	mask. The C++-side mechanism for the per-thread pinning that pairs with
915	`isolcpus`.
916	
917	### `rcu_nocbs` — `intro`
918	Linux boot parameter that offloads RCU (read-copy-update) callbacks off
919	the specified cores. Removes a class of kernel work from the HFT cores.
920	
921	### `SCHED_FIFO` — `intro`
922	Linux real-time scheduling class. A `SCHED_FIFO` thread runs until it
923	voluntarily blocks; preempts lower-priority work. Used for the strategy
924	thread.
925	
926	### SPSC ring buffer — `intro`
927	Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free queue using a power-of-two
928	circular array and atomic head/tail indices with release/acquire ordering.
929	The HFT-grade inter-thread communication primitive.
930	
931	### Synchronizes-with relationship — `intro`
932	The C++ memory-model term for the formal guarantee that a release-store on
933	one thread "synchronizes with" an acquire-load that reads its value on
934	another thread. The reason SPSC rings need release/acquire to be correct.
935	
936	### Thread pinning — `intro`
937	Binding a thread to a specific CPU core so the scheduler can't migrate it.
938	Eliminates cache invalidation from migration and is the in-program half of
939	`isolcpus`-based isolation.

943	## Added in Lesson 0011 (Low-Latency vs Ultra-Low-Latency)
944	
945	### Adverse selection (in latency context) — `intro`
946	Losing money systematically because faster participants see the same signal
947	microseconds before you and pick off the favorable side. The structural risk
948	of running at a lower tier than your venue's median competitor.
949	
950	### App-to-app latency — `intro`
951	Latency measured between two points inside your application code only
952	(e.g. signal extracted → decision made). Excludes wire and kernel. Useful
953	for internal optimization, not for competitive comparison.
954	
955	### ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) — `intro`
956	Custom silicon fabricated for one purpose. Faster than FPGAs but multi-
957	million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen logic. Tier 6 of the latency ladder;
958	only the largest desks justify it.
959	
960	### Hardware timestamp — `intro`
961	A nanosecond-resolution timestamp attached to a packet by the NIC or FPGA at
962	ingress/egress. The only trustworthy clock at ULL scales — immune to OS
963	scheduling and clock skew.
964	
965	### Inside-FPGA latency — `intro`
966	Latency measured between registers on a single FPGA, i.e. a fixed number of
967	clock cycles. At 250 MHz, 1 cycle = 4 ns. Fundamentally different unit than
968	wire-to-wire latency.
969	
970	### Jitter (latency variability) — `intro`
971	The variability of latency across events, often quoted as `p99.99 − p50` or
972	as the standard deviation. ULL systems are judged on jitter as much as on
973	median latency.
974	
975	### Latency ladder / tier — `intro`
976	The 6-rung industry mental model of trading-system latency, from Tier 0
977	(web app, ms) through Tier 6 (ASIC + microwave, ns + cross-market RF). Each
978	rung is ~10× more expensive than the one above.
979	
980	### Latency tail — `intro`
981	The high-percentile portion of the latency distribution (p99, p99.9,
982	p99.99). At HFT message rates, tail events happen multiple times per
983	second; the tail is what loses money, not the mean.
984	
985	### Low-latency (LL) — `intro`
986	Industry term for systems with microsecond-scale tick-to-trade (~1–100 µs).
987	Tuned C++, lock-free queues, kernel TCP. Tier 2 of the ladder.
988	
989	### Microwave / RF link — `intro`
990	Line-of-sight wireless link used for cross-market arbitrage. Light through
991	air ≈ 1.0c vs ~0.67c through glass — a few ms edge over a thousand km. The
992	basis of the Chicago↔NJ trading corridor.
993	
994	### One-way latency — `intro`
995	Time from event ingress to action emission, measured in one direction
996	(e.g. tick arrival → order on wire). Distinct from round-trip; both are
997	quoted in HFT and must be specified.
998	
999	### p50 / p99 / p99.99 — `intro`
1000	Quantiles of the latency distribution: 50%, 99%, 99.99% of events come in
1001	under this latency. HFT systems are evaluated on the higher percentiles.
1002	
1003	### Real-time (OS sense) — `intro`
1004	Bounded worst-case latency. Distinct from "fast" — a 10 ms deterministic
1005	system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems
1006	aim to be real-time first.
1007	
1008	### Round-trip latency — `intro`
1009	Time from event ingress to action egress through the full pipeline, including
1010	the order leaving your NIC. The headline tick-to-trade number in most
1011	benchmarks is wire-to-wire round-trip.
1012	
1013	### Strategy cadence — `intro`
1014	The natural decision rate of a strategy (per day, per second, per tick).
1015	The single most useful input to deciding what tier of latency the strategy
1016	needs.
1017	
1018	### TSC (Time-Stamp Counter) — `intro`
1019	x86 CPU register incremented every cycle. Read with `rdtsc` in ~10 ns;
1020	nanosecond resolution but needs `tsc_reliable` and per-core synchronization
1021	on multi-socket systems.
1022	
1023	### Ultra-low-latency (ULL) — `intro`
1024	Industry term for systems with nanosecond-scale tick-to-trade (~10 ns – 1
1025	µs). FPGA, kernel-bypass NIC, hardware timestamps, microwave links. Tiers
1026	3–6 of the ladder.
1027	
1028	### Wire-to-wire latency — `intro`
1029	Time from the last bit of an inbound packet arriving at the NIC to the
1030	first bit of an outbound order leaving the NIC. The most defensible
1031	endpoint pair for competitive benchmarking.

1050	### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
1051	Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
1052	and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
1053	are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.
1054	
1055	### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
1056	71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
1057	to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
1058	exchange data centers; not for long-haul.
1059	
1060	### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
1061	Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
1062	authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
1063	incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
1064	firms rent rather than build.
1065	
1066	### Fresnel zone — `intro`
1067	The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
1068	antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
1069	Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.
1070	
1071	### Great-circle distance — `intro`
1072	Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
1073	floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.
1074	
1075	### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
1076	Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
1077	photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
1078	bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
1079	on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.
1080	
1081	### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
1082	Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
1083	limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
1084	always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.

1086	### McKay Brothers — `intro`

1094	narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.
1095	
1096	### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
1097	The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1098	1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
1099	and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.

1101	### Rain fade — `intro`
1102	Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
1103	at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
1104	reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.

1107	Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
1108	slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
1109	silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave

1114	(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
1115	licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.

1125	40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower

1151	
1152	- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.

The Sharpe ratio

205

206 A unit-free measure of return per unit of risk. The textbook version uses 207 excess return over a risk-free rate; this repo uses the simpler "raw" 208 version (assumes risk-free = 0): 209

Maximum drawdown — the worst the curve ever felt

241

242 Drawdown at time t is the percentage drop from the running 243 peak so far: 244

245 246
247 DDt = equityt / maxs≤t(equitys) − 1 248 Always ≤ 0. The minimum over the whole period is the "max drawdown." 249
250 251

252 In code this is two lines: a running cumulative max, then a ratio: 253

cum      = (1 + ret).cumprod()       # 1 + cumulative growth path
256	roll_max = cum.cummax()                # running peak so far

261 Why care: Sharpe says nothing about shape. Two strategies can have 262 identical Sharpe and very different max drawdowns. Drawdown is the number 263 investors actually pull capital over. 264

265 266

CAGR — geometric annual growth, the honest version of "average return"

267

268 Two ways to summarize "what return did I earn per year on average": 269

270 271
272 APRsimple = mean(daily return) × 252 273 Arithmetic — ignores compounding 274
275 276
277 CAGR = (final / initial)252/N − 1 278 Geometric — what actually compounded to that final value 279
280 281

282 They are not the same number. CAGR < APRsimple 283 by an amount that grows with volatility (this is the 284 volatility drag: CAGR ≈ μ − σ²/2 in log terms). A 285 strategy with daily returns alternating +10% / −10% has APR ≈ 0 but 286 CAGR ≈ −1.005% per period — because two such days compound to 287 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, not 1.00. 4. Covariance matrix and the CUSUM statistic

292 293

Covariance — when assets move together

294

295 Variance generalizes to covariance when you have multiple 296 assets: 297

298 299
300 Σij = E[(ri − μi)(rj − μj)] 301 Σii = variance of asset i. Σij = how i and j co-move. 302
303 304

305 For a portfolio with weight vector w: 306

307 308
309 portfolio variance = wT Σ w 310
311 312

313 That single equation is why correlations matter: two highly-correlated 314 assets in a portfolio don't diversify you, no matter how good each one is 315 individually. The mean-variance optimizer (Lesson 0007's target) lives or 316 dies on a stable estimate of Σ. The repo estimates it as the sample covariance 317 of recent daily returns over a --cov_lookback window (default 90 days). 318

319 320

CUSUM — detecting a regime break

321

322 The cumulative sum (CUSUM) test detects when a time series 323 has drifted away from its mean — i.e. when something structurally changed. 324 Two running sums track upward and downward drift: 325

326 327
328 S+t = max(0, S+t−1 + (rt − μ) − k) 329
330 S−t = min(0, S−t−1 + (rt − μ) + k) 331 k is a "slack" parameter, typically a multiple of σ. Trigger when |S| crosses a threshold. 332
333 334

335 The repo uses CUSUM as one of four stress detectors in 336 walkforward_sim.py, with k = cusum_threshold × σ where 337 cusum_threshold defaults to 3. The intuition: small noise should 338 leave both running sums near zero; a sustained drift in either direction 339 pushes one of them past the threshold and signals a regime change. 340

CAGR vs APR (arithmetic mean × 252)

439

440 CAGR = geometric — what actually compounded. 441 APRsimple = mean × 252 — what arithmetic says. 442 APR is always ≥ CAGR. The gap is volatility drag ≈ σ²/2. 443 Quote CAGR to investors; quote both internally. 444

Volatility vs Variance

448

449 Variance = E[(r − μ)²]. Units: returns². 450 Volatility = √variance. Units: returns. People say "vol" 451 when they want a number they can compare to mean return (same units). 452 Variance is what mathematically adds across time; vol is what gets quoted. 453

458 Sharpe divides excess return by total standard deviation. 459 Sortino divides by downside deviation only 460 (treats upside vol as good). Sortino is kinder to strategies with 461 positively skewed returns; this repo computes only Sharpe. 462

466

467 A loss is realized P&L below your starting capital. 468 A drawdown is below your running peak — you can 469 have a 30% drawdown while still up 50% from your start. Investors 470 emotionally treat both as failures; drawdown is the harsher measure. 471

476 Sample uses (n−1) in the denominator (unbiased estimator from a sample). 477 Population uses n (when you have the whole population). For finite return 478 samples we want ddof=1. pandas defaults to 1; numpy defaults to 0. 479 Same word, different number. 480
